title: Traitor
full_review:
"I answer to God; we all do." So says a character in the astute espionage thriller "Traitor" (Overture), a study of conflicting loyalties and identities that probes significant moral problems about the use of violence on both sides of the war on terror.

 

The film's protagonist, deeply religious Muslim American Samir Horn (Don Cheadle, who also produced) finds himself at the conflict's center. A former U.S. special operations officer who worked with the multinational Muslim mujahedeen rebels to overthrow Soviet rule in Afghanistan, the Sudanese-born Horn is now suspected of having followed some of those former American allies onto the path of terrorism. In the film's opening scenes, he attempts to sell munitions to an Islamist cell in Yemen, only to be caught in a military raid and thrown into prison.

There he meets Omar (Said Taghmaoui), a dedicated jihadist who's impressed when he observes Horn give up his meal to a fellow prisoner victimized by a bully. Omar has been plotting to break out of prison and adjusts his plans to take Horn with him.

After the two make their way to southern France, Omar introduces Horn to his high-living patrons, Fareed (Aly Khan) and Nathir (Raad Rawi). Although initially offended by Fareed's un-Islamic taste for champagne -- quaffed under the excuse of needing to blend in with French society -- Horn is soon a trusted ally in the group's efforts to attack American interests.

Yet, as FBI agents Roy Clayton (Guy Pearce) and Max Archer (Neal McDonough) follow Horn's movements, their subject's ultimate allegiance remains ambiguous. Horn's in sporadic contact with Carter (Jeff Daniels), a rogue CIA operative, for instance, and when he turns the tables on one of his American pursuers, Horn passes up the chance to kill him.

Writer-director Jeffrey Nachmanoff's engaging film, based on a scenario conceived by co-executive producer Steve Martin, maintains a suspenseful story line while also exploring, through Cheadle's understated performance, Horn's interior struggle to follow the right path.

Avoiding Muslim stereotypes and easy answers to complex geopolitical issues, it upholds genuine faith, both Horn's and Clayton's (who, we learn, studied to be a Baptist minister before turning to the study of Arabic), against violent ideology merely cloaked by faith such as that followed by Fareed.

The film contains moderate action violence, one use of the F-word and some crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
